Meager

/MEE-ger/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Meager means deficient in size, amount, or quality — thin, small, and not enough.

The innkeeper served a meager dinner: a spoonful of rice and half a slice of bread.

Worked Example

For a full week of hauling crates on the docks, the worker received a meager pay envelope that barely covered his rent.

Meager fits because the pay is far too small for the work done — deficient in amount, falling well short of what would be adequate.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

paltry: Paltry means so small it reads as an insult from whoever offered it — a paltry raise, a paltry settlement — and it sneers at the giver. Meager is sadder than it is angry: a meager meal or salary is thin and inadequate, but the word passes no judgment on anyone's generosity.

skimpy: Skimpy means providing less than is needed, usually because someone cut corners — a skimpy portion, skimpy coverage. It hints that more could easily have been given. Meager describes plain inadequacy from any cause: a meager harvest after a drought skimped on nothing; there simply was not enough.

insufficient: Insufficient is the neutral, technical way to say not enough for the purpose — insufficient funds, insufficient evidence. It states a shortfall without imagery. Meager adds the picture: thin, small, and inadequate, a word you can almost see. An account balance is insufficient; the dinner on the table is meager.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

abundant: existing in large, plentiful amounts

generous: larger or fuller than expected

Where it sits · how far short of enough it falls — small → meager → pitiful

small vs. meager: A small lunch is simply not large; a meager lunch is too little to satisfy anyone.

pitiful vs. meager: A meager wage barely covers the basics; a pitiful one is so tiny it feels like an insult.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — meager

Root — meager: from Old French maigre, from Latin macer, 'thin, lean' — a thin, undernourished quality

Put it together

Put it together: Meager traveled from the Latin macer ('thin, lean') through Old French maigre into English. A word that first described a lean, underfed body came to describe anything too thin and too small — meals, wages, supplies, results.

Use the root in a new word: emaciated

Use the root in a new word: emaciated: The rescued horse was so emaciated that every one of its ribs showed.

Root Check

Word Choice

Neutral

Meager is a close cousin of scant, another word in this unit: both mean 'barely enough.' The nuance — meager stresses thin, inadequate quality or amount (a meager meal, a meager salary), while scant stresses falling just short of a needed amount (scant evidence, scant attention). Meager pairs most naturally with food, money, and resources.
